q: Does the paper's ABM-MC coupled model, when extended to FLASH-radiotherapy regimes (ultra-high dose rate, ~40 Gy/s), predict reduced fibrosis at matched total dose compared with conventional dose-rate delivery, and does this match preclinical FLASH lung-sparing data?
basis: The current model uses per-fraction dose delivery with 24h inter-fraction dynamics. FLASH sparing is a live clinical/preclinical question with mechanistic hypotheses involving transient oxygen depletion and modified TGF-beta signalling, both of which the ABM's cytokine/senescence machinery could in principle test. The paper does not address dose rate.
next_steps: 1) Extend the BioDynaMo ABM's LQ kernel to include a dose-rate term (e.g., temporal integration of dose over instantaneous rate, coupled to a transient oxygen field). 2) Recompile and run 1-fx conventional vs FLASH (matched total dose) at 10, 20, 30 Gy, 10 replicates. 3) Compare late DeltaECM(D) and FSU survival against Vozenin et al. and Favaudon et al. mouse-lung FLASH datasets. Free endpoints: use published FLASH lung-fibrosis endpoints from open-access literature; no wet-lab needed.

q: Can the ABM's cell-state definitions (healthy AEC2, damaged, senescent, myofibroblast) be re-parameterised from single-cell RNA-seq atlases of irradiated lung (e.g., Strunz et al. Nat Commun 2020, Riemondy et al.), and do the omics-informed cell-state transition rates change the predicted DeltaECM(D) shape?
basis: The paper's cell-state transition rates (damaged to senescent at 0.25/day, phag fraction 0.4, phag index 1) are hand-tuned or from prior work, not from single-cell data. Modern scRNA-seq of irradiated lung provides transition-rate priors via pseudotime analysis. This tests whether the ABM's qualitative behaviour is robust to biologically-grounded parameter shifts, or whether tuning drives the sigmoid ED50.
next_steps: 1) Download Strunz et al. GEO GSE141259 (bleomycin lung fibrosis scRNA-seq, comparable injury). 2) Fit pseudotime transition rates for AEC2 to damaged to senescent to apoptotic using CellRank or Monocle3. 3) Replace ABM constants with pseudotime-derived rates. 4) Re-run 1-fx dose sweep. 5) Compare shifted ED50 to the paper's. Free endpoints: GEO data + open-source scRNA-seq packages.

q: How well does the model's predicted DeltaECM(D) map to specific clinical patient cohorts (e.g., stage III NSCLC post-SBRT, thoracic lymphoma post-mantle-field), and does the model's fibrosis-index predict grade-2+ radiation pneumonitis in the QUANTEC datasets?
basis: The paper compares to preclinical Zhou et al. mouse fibrosis-index only. Clinical translation to human RILF (QUANTEC MLD/V20 metrics, pneumonitis grading) is the natural next step. This tests whether the mechanistic ABM adds predictive value over statistical NTCP models.
next_steps: 1) Extract QUANTEC MLD (mean lung dose) and V20 (volume at 20+ Gy) values from Marks et al. 2010 review Table 2. 2) Run the ABM at each cohort's MLD as an equivalent uniform dose. 3) Compute RSI at 6 and 12 months post-RT. 4) ROC against published pneumonitis grade-2+ rates. 5) Compare AUC to the Lyman-Kutcher-Burman NTCP baseline. Free endpoints: QUANTEC is open-access.

q: How sensitive is the fibrosis-index prediction to AEC2 cell-cycle length assumptions (currently implicit in the daily proliferation gate), and does variability in this parameter explain the between-patient variance in RILF risk?
basis: The ABM's repopulation term is gated by ECM stiffness (exp of negative ECM_excess over threshold) but assumes a single homeostatic proliferation timescale. Human AEC2 cell-cycle length varies with age, comorbidity, and prior injury. This is a candidate mechanistic source of patient heterogeneity in RILF.
next_steps: 1) Parameterise the proliferation-gate timescale as tau_prol in {2, 4, 7, 14} days. 2) Run 1-fx sweep at each tau, 10 reps. 3) Compute the coefficient of variation of DeltaECM at fixed dose across tau. 4) Compare to clinical between-patient RILF variance from open cohort data. 5) If tau explains most of the variance, this becomes a testable clinical biomarker (e.g., pre-RT AEC2 turnover assay). Free endpoints: existing surrogate + published RILF variance stats.

q: Can machine-learning parameter identification from serial post-RT clinical CT images (via radiomics-derived ECM-density surrogates) recover the paper's ABM parameters, and could this enable per-patient ABM personalisation?
basis: Serial CT after thoracic RT shows evolving density changes that correlate with fibrosis. If a neural surrogate of the ABM can be inverted from CT-derived features, the ABM becomes personalisable without wet-lab measurement. This is the direct translational endpoint the paper gestures at but does not attempt.
next_steps: 1) Build a neural surrogate of abm_lite (or the full ABM) mapping {alpha, beta, phag_fraction, k_mf_grow} to DeltaECM(t) trajectories. Train on 10k Latin-hypercube ABM runs. 2) Download the TCIA NSCLC-Radiomics collection (open, DICOM). 3) Extract time-series HU-density change in the treated volume. 4) Invert the surrogate: fit patient-specific ABM parameters that reproduce each patient's CT trajectory. 5) Test whether patient-level parameters cluster by pneumonitis grade. Free endpoints: TCIA is open; PyRadiomics is open-source; training compute is one GPU-day.
